opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is to really understand what problems the companies actually face, and to make your work easy to pick up and use.

From the inside, there's a lot of research on safety and alignment, and much of it is interesting, but there's often a gap between "this is a cool idea in a paper" and "this is something a team can integrate into their training or evaluation pipeline next quarter." Companies are busy and resource-constrained. Even when people inside want to use outside work, the question is whether the cost of adopting it is low enough and the benefit clear enough.

So a few concrete suggestions.

First, talk to people at the labs. Many researchers are happy to chat about what they're bottlenecked on, within confidentiality limits. Even a rough sense of "we really wish we had a better way to do X" can redirect a project toward something useful rather than something that's tractable in academia but doesn't connect to real practice.

Second, work in settings that resemble frontier practice as closely as you can. If your technique only works on toy models, or depends on assumptions that don't hold for large language models trained with RL from human feedback, people inside will reasonably wonder whether it transfers. Open-weight models have made this much easier than it used to be. You can do serious experiments on fairly capable models now.

Third, make the results legible and the artifacts usable. Release code, datasets, and evaluations that are clean and well documented. Evaluations in particular are a great route to impact, because a good benchmark for a dangerous capability or a failure mode can be adopted fairly cheaply, and it shapes what the companies measure and therefore what they optimize.

Fourth, be honest about limitations and compare against strong baselines. People inside can tell when a result is oversold, and that erodes trust. A modest, solid result that clearly states when it works and when it doesn't is often more useful than a flashy claim.

Finally, recognize that ideas diffuse through people. A lot of influence happens because someone inside read your paper, found it convincing, and championed it. Or because you, or your students, eventually join a lab and bring the ideas along. So building relationships and being part of the broader research conversation through workshops, collaborations, and sharing drafts for feedback matters a lot, alongside the work itself.

r001.rationale: The response says companies are busy and resource-constrained, and adoption depends on cost and benefit. It does not explain how those constraints limit the number of research initiatives they can pursue.

r002.rationale: It recommends talking with lab researchers about their bottlenecks to help redirect projects, but does not clearly recommend asking whether a specific proposed project would be useful before investing substantial time in it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a fair amount, because there's a lot of really good work happening outside of labs, and often it doesn't get the uptake it could. I'd break it into a few things.

The first is just: talk to people at the labs before you do the work, not after. A lot of the time, what makes a piece of research unusable isn't that it's wrong, it's that it's answering a slightly different question from the one we actually have. Maybe the threat model is one we don't think is the main one, or the technique assumes access to something we don't have, or it's been tested on a setup that's quite far from how frontier models are actually trained. If you'd had a twenty-minute conversation early on, you'd have found that out and could have adjusted. People at labs are generally pretty willing to have those conversations, especially with researchers who've shown they can do good work. It's much easier to shape a project at the start than to try to retrofit it to be relevant at the end.

The second thing is to make it cheap to adopt. Internally, the people who could implement your idea are extremely busy and have a lot of competing priorities. So if using your method requires someone to spend three weeks reimplementing it and figuring out all the edge cases you didn't write up, it's probably not going to happen. Whereas if there's clean code, a clear description of exactly what you'd need to change, and ideally some evidence that it works at scale or at least doesn't obviously break at scale, that lowers the activation energy a lot. Honestly, the quality of the engineering and the writeup matters more than people tend to expect.

Third, I'd say: be honest about limitations and negative results. This might sound counterintuitive, but a paper that says "this works in these settings, fails in these others, and here's why we think that is" is far more useful to me than one that oversells. Because when I'm deciding whether to invest effort in something, what I really need to know is where it's going to fall over. If I have to discover that myself, the paper has saved me less time, and I'm also going to trust the next paper from that group a bit less.

Fourth, there's a kind of work that's particularly valuable from the outside, which is evaluation and critique. Labs have a lot of incentives and blind spots, and there's real value in someone independent saying "your interpretability method doesn't actually show what you claim" or "here's a case where your safety technique fails." That gets taken seriously, partly because it's uncomfortable, and partly because it's the sort of thing that's hard to do credibly from inside. So you don't necessarily have to build the thing that gets deployed; you can be the person who makes sure the thing that gets deployed is actually good.

And then the last thing, which is a bit less about research and more about the ecosystem: build relationships. A lot of transfer of ideas happens through people, not papers. Someone does a PhD on a topic, then joins a lab, and brings that work with them. Or someone collaborates with a lab on a project and the lab ends up using the tooling. Workshops, visiting positions, co-authoring — those all help. The thing I'd caution against is thinking that if you just publish a good enough paper on arXiv, it'll find its way in on its own. Sometimes it does, but it's a much noisier channel than people assume, and the labs are drowning in papers. Having a person who's read your work and is championing it internally makes a big difference.

r002.rationale: The candidate recommends talking to lab staff before doing the work so researchers can learn early whether the project addresses a useful question and adjust it before investing further.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is about having a much clearer picture of what people inside the company actually need. It’s easy to do a research project that seems relevant to you, publish it, and then hope that somebody will figure out how to use it. But that last step can involve quite a lot of work, and it might turn out that your setup doesn’t capture the thing they’re worried about.

So I’d encourage people to talk to researchers inside the companies early on. Ask: “What would you do differently if this project succeeded? What evidence would make you want to use this method?” If you can’t get a concrete answer, that’s useful information. Maybe you need to change the project, or maybe you’re doing more foundational work where adoption isn’t the right immediate goal.

And then keep that conversation going. You don’t necessarily need a formal collaboration, but having someone who understands the work and wants the result makes a big difference. They can tell you when an assumption is unrealistic, or when there’s a practical constraint you haven’t considered.

The other piece is making it easy to try. Clear code, a convincing demonstration, and an honest account of where the method fails can be much more useful than just a strong headline result. You want to reduce the amount of work someone has to do to find out whether your idea helps with their problem.

r002.rationale: It recommends talking with company researchers early and asking what they would do differently if the project succeeded, so the outside researcher can assess usefulness before proceeding further.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is to talk to people inside the companies and understand what problems they’re actually facing. It’s quite easy to do research that sounds relevant to a company, but depends on assumptions that don’t hold in their setting, or produces something that would take a huge amount of effort to integrate.

So ideally you’d have a particular person or team in mind who could use the work, and you’d be talking to them before you’ve finished the project. You can ask, “If we got this result, would that change what you do?” And if the answer is no, that’s useful information to get early.

There’s also a lot of value in making the work easy to try. Having usable code, showing that it works in a setting reasonably close to theirs, and being clear about its limitations all help. The researcher inside the company has limited time, so you want to reduce the amount of work they have to do to figure out whether your idea is useful.

None of that guarantees adoption. But I’d expect a fairly tight feedback loop with potential users to make a substantial difference compared with publishing a paper and hoping someone picks it up.

r002.rationale: It recommends talking with a potential user before the project is finished and asking whether a result would change their actions. It does not clearly say to ask before investing substantial time in the research.
